data.name: Devil In The Capital
data.detailed_description:
With the nationalization of the Iran oil industry and the establishment of the national government in 1952, the hands of the British had been cut off from the Iranian oil. Notwithstanding this, they try everything in their power to defeat the national government. Amid foreign and domestic acts of sabotage and attempts to overthrow the government in Tehran and Southern Iran, hidden forces in Northern Iran join to steal the Iranian oil. This is aggravated by the killing of the representative of Rasht, who was an advocate of the national movement, and of a number of police officers in Rasht and others dispatched from Tehran. Thus, detective Mohammad Afshar is dispatched to Rasht to unravel mysteries about these actions which were against the national interests. In addition to learning about a number of gruesome murders, he discovers efforts to divert people’s attention to multiple crimes to prepare the ground for a coup. In addition to identifying the murderers, Afshar has to deal with the evident treason that is being shaped.

• Game features

1- A fascinating and engaging story in a film noir setting similar to that of serial killing stories
2- Loyal to the Adventure genre, more than 12 mini games and tens of environmental puzzles
3- Tens of graphic documents, newspapers, short stories, and old advertisements
4- Narrating the story in more than 20 locations and 65 backgrounds with utmost 2D detail
5- 27 characters with more than 150 pages of captivating dialogue
6- More than 20 minutes of motion comics for a more precise narration of the story
7- 60 minutes of engaging film noir music
8- 95 pages of completely interactive daily notes by the detective
9- More than 5 hours of gameplay

data.short_description: With the death of the second police detective in one of the northern Iranian cities, the total number of victims adds up to 5. It’s as if no one, whether the general public or high-ranking political figures and even detectives from the police office are safe from the murderer(s).

reviews.review:
Devil In The Capital is a narrative-focused point-and-click adventure that builds its identity around murder, political intrigue, and a historical period rarely represented in video games. Developed by RSK Entertainment and published by Strategy First, the game takes place in Iran in 1952, during the turbulent period surrounding the nationalization of the country's oil industry. Rather than treating history as a simple backdrop, the story incorporates political uncertainty and competing national interests directly into its mystery. The result is an investigative adventure that combines traditional puzzle solving with the atmosphere of a noir crime story.

Players assume the role of Mohammad Afshar, a detective drawn into a disturbing investigation in Rasht. A representative associated with the national movement has been murdered, and the situation becomes increasingly alarming when police officers and investigators sent from Tehran also become victims. What initially appears to be a sequence of killings gradually reveals connections to something considerably larger. Afshar begins uncovering signs of organized political activity, sabotage, attempted oil theft, and a potential coup. This gradual expansion from a local murder case into a conspiracy affecting the country gives the narrative a stronger sense of consequence.

The historical setting is arguably the game's most compelling quality. The struggle surrounding Iranian oil, political sovereignty, and foreign interests creates a believable foundation for paranoia and suspicion. Afshar must operate in an environment where motives are rarely straightforward and where criminal acts may hide political objectives. The story frequently emphasizes the difficulty of separating ordinary crimes from deliberate attempts to destabilize the country. This approach makes the mystery feel different from the more familiar mansions, fictional cities, and supernatural settings commonly associated with point-and-click adventures.

Gameplay remains firmly rooted in the conventions of the genre. Players examine locations, interact with objects, investigate evidence, communicate with different characters, and complete puzzles or mini-games to advance the story. More than a dozen mini-games are incorporated throughout the adventure, adding variety between conversations and exploration. The puzzles generally serve the progression of the investigation rather than turning the game into a demanding puzzle marathon. This makes the experience relatively approachable, although experienced adventure players looking for highly complicated deductions may consider some portions straightforward.

Conversation is especially important because Devil In The Capital contains a sizable cast of characters and a large amount of dialogue. Afshar encounters people who contribute information, suspicions, political perspectives, and possible connections to the crimes. Working through these conversations is essential to understanding how the different pieces of the conspiracy fit together. The large amount of written material gives the narrative considerable detail, but it also means that patience is required. Players who enjoy reading and following lengthy investigations are likely to appreciate this approach more than those who prefer constant action.

Documents play an equally significant role in creating the world. Newspapers, written stories, advertisements, investigative material, and other illustrated documents help communicate both clues and historical context. Afshar also keeps extensive interactive notes related to his investigation. These records provide useful context while reinforcing the fantasy of working through a complicated detective case. Instead of relying entirely on spoken exposition, the game encourages players to absorb information through the materials scattered throughout its environments.

The presentation complements this slower investigative structure. Devil In The Capital uses detailed 2D artwork across numerous locations and backgrounds, giving the experience the appearance of an illustrated crime novel. Its environments are more concerned with establishing atmosphere and historical character than showcasing technical complexity. The locations help convey the sense of exploring a country experiencing considerable political tension, while the darker visual direction supports the noir influences behind the story.

Motion-comic sequences are also used during important narrative moments. These scenes give major developments a more cinematic presentation while remaining consistent with the game's illustrated visual style. They are accompanied by a substantial soundtrack influenced by film noir, which adds tension to exploration and investigation. Since much of the gameplay involves reading, searching, and talking rather than combat or fast movement, the music is particularly important for maintaining suspense. The combination of artwork, cinematic sequences, and music gives the adventure a stronger personality than its conventional mechanics alone might provide.

The game's relatively compact duration works both in its favor and against it. The mystery can be completed without the enormous commitment required by many sprawling narrative games, making it suitable for players wanting a focused detective adventure. At the same time, the considerable amount of dialogue, historical information, documents, puzzles, and political exposition can make the experience feel dense. Its generally linear progression also means that replay value is limited once the central mystery has been solved. There is more incentive to carefully explore everything during the first playthrough than to immediately begin another.

Another limitation is that players expecting a sophisticated detective simulation may find the investigation more guided than anticipated. Devil In The Capital is primarily an authored story in which the player helps Afshar uncover predetermined revelations. It does not provide extensive freedom to accuse anyone, radically change the investigation, or create numerous alternative solutions. Its strengths therefore depend less on player agency and more on atmosphere, storytelling, historical context, and the satisfaction of gradually discovering how seemingly separate events are connected.

Despite those limitations, Devil In The Capital remains an interesting example of how a familiar adventure-game formula can become distinctive through setting and subject matter. Its depiction of 1950s Iran gives the mystery cultural and political dimensions rarely encountered in the genre. The mixture of serial killings, national politics, espionage-like intrigue, sabotage, and conspiracy creates enough momentum to keep the investigation engaging, particularly for players interested in historical fiction.

Overall, Devil In The Capital is best approached as an interactive historical noir mystery rather than an advanced detective simulator. RSK Entertainment uses conventional point-and-click mechanics as a framework for a much more unusual story, while publisher Strategy First presents an adventure aimed at players comfortable with substantial reading and deliberate pacing. The illustrated environments, extensive dialogue, documents, mini-games, atmospheric soundtrack, motion-comic sequences, and politically charged storyline combine into an experience with clear individuality. Its linearity and text-heavy structure may restrict its appeal, but the uncommon setting and ambitious narrative make it worthwhile for enthusiasts of story-driven adventure games. 

Rating: 6/10
